newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. AFRICAN MPS SEEK TARIFF POLICY REVIEW.
newsitem.headline: S. AFRICAN MPS SEEK TARIFF POLICY REVIEW.

text.p: The impact of tariff reductions on South African manufacturing has not been adequately assessed, parliament's trade and industry committee says in a report due for ratification on Friday.

Reporting on two days of public hearings in Pretoria recently, the committee says in a draft report there is significant disagreement between business and labour on the one side and government on the other about the impact of the Trade and Industry Ministry's tariff reduction programme.
"There is a significant degree of concern that tariff reductions are harming existing industry unduly," the committee says in the report.
Committee chairman Rob Davies said the report would be adopted formally on Friday and he did not expect any significant changes to be made.

The committee recommends that the statutory National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) grouping business, labour and government should review the government's tariff and industrial policies.
The review should address the impact of tariff reductions required by the World Trade Organisation on employment, competitiveness and women.

"Further consideration (should) be given to...the link between tariff reductions and exchange rate depreciations," the committee says in a reference to the nearly 20 percent devaluation of the rand this year.
The report calls for a crackdown on dumping, which, fuelled by weak border controls, is flooding South African markets with cheap goods from abroad.
"Further measures (should) be taken urgently to improve the capacity of our customs department to administer tariffs and effectively control our borders," it says.
The report suggests a system of tax penalties and incentives to boost average spending on training from the current 2.5 percent of payroll to the international norm of four to seven percent.
It recommends a "Buy South African" campaign for goods certified of international standard and a Council for Economic Planning to consider industrial policy in a context of broader economic policy.
The government is not obliged to implement the committee's views, but is likely to take them seriously.
